questions.question: What is Saadat Hasan Manto primarily known for? (U)(CO3) a. Writing romantic poetry b. Painting abstract art. c. bold and unflinching portrayal of society d. blatant criticism of religious practice
questions.solution_html:
• The short story "Khol Do" ("Open It") by Saadat Hasan Manto - a powerful and
  • disturbing portrayal of the psychological devastation caused by war and the horrors of
  • Partition in 1947 - uses the tragic fate of a young girl, Sakina, and the despair of her father
  • Sirajuddin, to reveal how deeply war can scar the human mind and soul.
  • Loss of identity and humanity – Sakina, a victim of rape and severe trauma - loses touch
  • with normal emotional or social responses. When the doctor says "Khol do" (open it)
  • intending it as an instruction for the window, Sakina responds by instinctively loosening
  • her shalwar cord — showing how she has been conditioned by repeated abuse – this
  • moment captures the brutal destruction of her sense of self and autonomy.
  • Mental breakdown of the father - Sirajuddin's psychological torment central to the story
  • loses his wife in the chaos of Partition - obsessively searches for his daughter - his hope
  • desperation, and final joy upon seeing her move are tragically misplaced — he interprets
  • her movement as life returning, unaware of what she has endured - inability to grasp the
  • extent of her trauma shows the psychological denial and helplessness war inflicts on
  • survivors.
  • Dehumanization of victims - soldiers who rescue Sakina are initially seen as saviours
  • later implied they are her abusers - war corrupts – protectors turned into predators - moral
  • decay - reveals how war dehumanizes individuals, blurring the lines between right and
  • wrong, protector and violator.
  • Symbolism of life and speech - Sakina is silent, a symbol of countless voiceless victims.
  • When she finally responds to “Khol do,” it’s not a return to consciousness, but a
  • conditioned, tragic reflex. Her silence speaks volumes about psychological trauma
  • sometimes so deep that it silences the soul. (CO3)

questions.final_answer: sometimes so deep that it silences the soul. (CO3)

questions.question: What message does Bhasa convey about the nature of victory and defeat?
questions.solution_html:
• Bhasa in “The Shattered Thigh” questions the assumptions about dharma and adharma
  • dramatizes the mace duel between Bhima and Duryodhana at the end of the
  • Kurukshethra war. Krishna’s interference changed the course of the Kurukshethra war.
  • When Bhima was about to lose, Krishna signals him about Duryodhana’ s thigh. Bhima
  • strikes Duryodhana’s thigh and defeats him which is against the rules of ‘dharma’ - this
  • incident significant in stripping away the glory of Kurukshethra war as a war based on
  • dharma - play questions the futility of pride and the devastating impact of war.
  • Duryodhana presented with a tinge of tragic heroism - his characterization deviates from
  • the conventional image of the antagonist of The Mahabharata - victory and defeat are
  • relative and purely context bound - conflict arises between sense of duty and
  • righteousness - Bhima wins against Duryodhana but cannot escape the indictment of
  • violating the rules of war - the very idea of ‘victory’ in war sounds meaningless.
  • (CO2)
questions.final_answer: (CO2)

questions.question: Does Bhasa present Duryodhana as a villain seeking redemption, or as a noble warrior accepting his fate?
questions.solution_html:
• Bhasa moves away from the traditional "evil" portrayal, framing Duryodhana as a tragic hero rather
  • than a spiteful antagonist - He does not complain about Bhima’s "foul play" (hitting below the belt).
  • He accepts his broken thighs as the inevitable result of fate and the war - His interaction with his
  • son, Durjaya, shows a tender, fatherly side. He tells his son to abandon the old hatreds, prioritizing
  • the child's peace over his own ego. - When Ashwatthama wants to continue the slaughter of the
  • Pandavas, Duryodhana stops him, signaling that his thirst for blood has ended. He views his death
  • not as a punishment, but as a warrior’s transition. He dies with a vision of heaven, signifying he has
  • achieved the status of a noble hero.
